{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"Choice screens are not market choice.

A choice screen is often presented as a small act of consumer freedom. Show several search engines, browsers, payment services, or other tools, and let people select one. The arrangement sounds modest and fair. But before the screen appears, someone has decided which options deserve a place on it, which order they occupy, and what happens when a person skips the decision. That’s where the market power remains.

The screen isn’t the market. It’s a doorway built by the company controlling the device, operating system, or service (the gatekeeper). The gatekeeper chooses the room of possible choices—a room whose walls can be invisible to the person standing outside it. A tool left outside that room can’t compete for attention on equal terms, however useful it may be.

This matters because visibility is part of distribution—a fact that is easy to miss when the interface makes selection look neutral. A developer may build a capable product, but a user will encounter it only if it can reach the relevant menu, store, prompt, or default setting (a browser, operating system, or marketplace). The person designing that interface can narrow the field before anyone makes a selection. A list can therefore look plural while reflecting one institution’s judgment about what counts as available.

Defaults do even more work. If the first option is already selected, many people will keep it. If changing the selection requires another screen, another download, or a warning about compatibility, the practical cost of choosing rises. The user may still be free to act—but the path of least resistance has been engineered in advance (the first screen).

That isn’t a trivial distinction. A default can shape habits, data flows, developer revenue, and the information a person sees over time. It can also make the incumbent appear stronger than it is. The product at the top receives more attention, which produces more use; more use attracts more developers; more developers make the product harder to leave. A selection made in seconds can reinforce a position built over years.

Supporters of choice screens may point to the act of selection itself. The user can choose, and that’s better than having no visible alternatives. That improvement matters. But it doesn’t answer who controls the list, the ranking, the defaults, or the consequences of refusing them. A restaurant doesn’t become independent of its owner merely because diners may pick among the dishes printed on its menu (for example).

The distinction becomes sharper when the gatekeeper supplies several options that depend on the same underlying infrastructure. A screen may offer variety at the surface while preserving control over payment rules, technical access, data portability, or distribution fees underneath. The names change; the bargaining position doesn’t. Developers are still asking the same company for permission to reach users.

What happens when the preferred tool is already installed, integrated into the account, and described as the safer choice? Does a person really compare alternatives, or are they accepting the decision that required the least effort? The answer will vary by context, but a policy that treats every click as an independent market test will miss the structure around the click.

A meaningful remedy would change that structure. It would require gatekeepers to disclose who selected the listed options and how the order was determined. It would limit discriminatory placement and require defaults that are genuinely neutral (rather than a single company’s product placed first). It would make switching practical through interoperability, data portability, and access to distribution channels on fair terms.

The remedy should also address the options that never appear. A developer should have a way to reach users without first winning approval from the same institution whose power the screen is supposed to restrain. That may require transparent eligibility rules, independent oversight, and a process for challenging exclusion. A list is accountable only when its boundaries are accountable too.

We should judge these screens by the power they redistribute, not by the number of buttons they display. Our concern isn’t whether a user may tap an alternative; it’s whether developers and users can act without accepting the gatekeeper’s terms as the price of entry. A meaningful choice screen would open the market beyond the menu. structured_output.draft:
Choice screens are not market choice.

A choice screen is often presented as a small act of consumer freedom. Show several search engines, browsers, payment services, or other tools, and let people select one. The arrangement sounds modest and fair. But before the screen appears, someone has decided which options deserve a place on it, which order they occupy, and what happens when a person skips the decision. That’s where the market power remains.

The screen isn’t the market. It’s a doorway built by the company controlling the device, operating system, or service (the gatekeeper). The gatekeeper chooses the room of possible choices—a room whose walls can be invisible to the person standing outside it. A tool left outside that room can’t compete for attention on equal terms, however useful it may be.

This matters because visibility is part of distribution—a fact that is easy to miss when the interface makes selection look neutral. A developer may build a capable product, but a user will encounter it only if it can reach the relevant menu, store, prompt, or default setting (a browser, operating system, or marketplace). The person designing that interface can narrow the field before anyone makes a selection. A list can therefore look plural while reflecting one institution’s judgment about what counts as available.

Defaults do even more work. If the first option is already selected, many people will keep it. If changing the selection requires another screen, another download, or a warning about compatibility, the practical cost of choosing rises. The user may still be free to act—but the path of least resistance has been engineered in advance (the first screen).

That isn’t a trivial distinction. A default can shape habits, data flows, developer revenue, and the information a person sees over time. It can also make the incumbent appear stronger than it is. The product at the top receives more attention, which produces more use; more use attracts more developers; more developers make the product harder to leave. A selection made in seconds can reinforce a position built over years.

Supporters of choice screens may point to the act of selection itself. The user can choose, and that’s better than having no visible alternatives. That improvement matters. But it doesn’t answer who controls the list, the ranking, the defaults, or the consequences of refusing them. A restaurant doesn’t become independent of its owner merely because diners may pick among the dishes printed on its menu (for example).

The distinction becomes sharper when the gatekeeper supplies several options that depend on the same underlying infrastructure. A screen may offer variety at the surface while preserving control over payment rules, technical access, data portability, or distribution fees underneath. The names change; the bargaining position doesn’t. Developers are still asking the same company for permission to reach users.

What happens when the preferred tool is already installed, integrated into the account, and described as the safer choice? Does a person really compare alternatives, or are they accepting the decision that required the least effort? The answer will vary by context, but a policy that treats every click as an independent market test will miss the structure around the click.

A meaningful remedy would change that structure. It would require gatekeepers to disclose who selected the listed options and how the order was determined. It would limit discriminatory placement and require defaults that are genuinely neutral (rather than a single company’s product placed first). It would make switching practical through interoperability, data portability, and access to distribution channels on fair terms.

The remedy should also address the options that never appear. A developer should have a way to reach users without first winning approval from the same institution whose power the screen is supposed to restrain. That may require transparent eligibility rules, independent oversight, and a process for challenging exclusion. A list is accountable only when its boundaries are accountable too.

We should judge these screens by the power they redistribute, not by the number of buttons they display. Our concern isn’t whether a user may tap an alternative; it’s whether developers and users can act without accepting the gatekeeper’s terms as the price of entry. A meaningful choice screen would open the market beyond the menu. Anything less merely gives concentrated power a friendlier interface.
